extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students (or contest/olympiad students) learning introductory ring theory/abstract algebra
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory chapter material defining rings, ideals, quotient rings, and common classes of rings (fields, integral domains, PIDs, Noetherian rings, UFDs, Euclidean domains), with theorems, examples, and exercises to build intuition and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonempty subset I ⊆ R is an ideal if it is closed under addition, and for each x ∈ I, rx ∈ I for all r ∈ R. It is proper if I ≠ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: r need not be in I (so this is stronger than being merely closed under multiplication). In noncommutative rings one also needs xr ∈ I (two-sided ideal). Examples: 5Z ⊆ Z is an ideal (kernel of reduction mod 5). Exercises and remarks: kernels of homomorphisms are ideals; check closure and absorption properties when verifying an ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kernel ↔ Ideal (characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let R be a ring and I ⊊ R. Then I is the kernel of some homomorphism if and only if it’s an ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: form the quotient ring S = {r + I | r ∈ R} (cosets) with operations well-defined; the surjective homomorphism R → S has kernel exactly I. Suggested exercise: check multiplication is well-defined using absorption property of I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotient ring R/I (definition & intuition)
rubrics_metrics.description: R/I := {r + I | r ∈ R}, the ring of cosets under the relation r1 ∼ r2 iff r1 − r2 ∈ I. Intuitively, R/I is what we get when we declare elements of I to be zero (we 'mod out by I').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of modding out as declaring elements of I zero (e.g. modding out by 5Z gives Z/5Z). Beware: you must check addition and multiplication on cosets are well-defined. Examples: Z[x]/(x) ≅ Z (send x to 0), Z[x]/(x−3) ≅ Z (evaluate at 3), Z[x]/(x−3,5) ≅ Z/5Z (evaluate at 3 mod 5). Notation: x ≡ y (mod I) means x−y ∈ I.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generated ideal (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal generated by elements x1, ..., xn ∈ R is denoted (x1, x2, ..., xn) and equals {r1 x1 + ··· + rn xn | ri ∈ R}. It is the smallest ideal containing the xi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: 'sealed box and shake' — all R-linear combinations. Applies also to infinite generating sets provided only finitely many coefficients are nonzero. Examples: (n)=nZ in Z; (x) in Z[x] consists of polynomials with zero constant term; (x,5) in Z[x] are polynomials whose constant term is divisible by 5. Exercise: verify the stated set is an ideal (closed under addition and absorbs multiplication).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper ideal ⇐⇒ contains no units (Proposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an ideal I ⊆ R, I is proper (I ≠ R) if and only if it contains no units of R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof sketch: if I contains a unit u, then 1 = u·u^{-1} ∈ I, so I = R. Conversely, if I contains no units, it cannot be all of R. Consequence: fields have exactly two ideals: (0) and K.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal ideal and principal ideal domain (PID)
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal generated by a single element (x) is called principal (consists of all multiples of x). A ring in which every ideal is principal is called a principal ideal ring; an integral domain where all ideals are principal is called a principal ideal domain (PID).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Z is a PID (every ideal is (n)). Z[x] is not a PID (e.g. (x,2015) is not principal). For a field k, k[x] is a PID. Use Bézout-type arguments to show polynomial rings over fields are PIDs. Practical take: PIDs let you take gcds of collections of elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian ring (equivalent definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ring R is Noetherian iff every ideal of R is finitely generated. Equivalently, there does not exist an infinite ascending chain of ideals I1 ⊊ I2 ⊊ I3 ⊊ ··· (ascending chain condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/non-examples: R = Z[x1,x2,...] is non-Noetherian because I=(x1,x2,...) is not finitely generated and yields an ascending chain (x1) ⊊ (x1,x2) ⊊ ···. The Hilbert basis theorem: if R is Noetherian then R[x] is Noetherian (hence polynomial rings in finitely many variables over a Noetherian ring are Noetherian). Importance: most rings encountered in practice are Noetherian; key in algebraic geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field (definition & ideal consequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A field K is a nontrivial ring in which every nonzero element is a unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate consequence: a field has exactly two ideals: (0) and K; (0) is maximal. Example: Q, R, C. Exercise: show fields are Noetherian (trivially) and integral domains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral domain (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A nontrivial ring with no zero divisors (i.e., if ab = 0 then either a = 0 or b = 0) is called an integral domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Z, R[x], Z[x]. Non-example: Z/15Z (3·5 ≡ 0). The trivial ring 0 is not considered an integral domain. Relation to primes: R/I is an integral domain iff I is prime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime ideal (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper ideal I ⊊ R is prime if whenever xy ∈ I, either x ∈ I or y ∈ I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: mirrors 'p prime ⇒ p|xy ⇒ p|x or p|y' for integers. Examples: (7) in Z is prime; (8) in Z is not; (x) in Z[x] is prime; (x^2) in Z[x] is not. Useful theorem: I is prime ⇐⇒ R/I is an integral domain. Exercise: identify primes/non-primes in examples such as (3,x) in Z[x], (5) in Z[i] (not prime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximal ideal (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proper ideal I of R is maximal if it is not contained in any other proper ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization: I is maximal ⇐⇒ R/I is a field. Consequence: every maximal ideal is prime (since fields are integral domains). Examples: (7) is maximal in Z; (x,5) is maximal in Z[x] because modding out by x and 5 yields F5; (x) in Z[x] is prime but not maximal (R/I ≅ Z). Exercise: use quotienting to check maximality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of fractions (Frac(R))
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an integral domain R, Frac(R) consists of elements a/b (a,b ∈ R, b ≠ 0) with a/b ∼ c/d iff bc = ad. Addition and multiplication are defined as for rational numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction turns an integral domain into its smallest containing field. Examples: Frac(Z)=Q; Frac(k[x]) = k(x) (field of rational functions). Gaussian rationals Q(i) = Frac(Z[i]). Guidance: check equivalence relation and well-defined operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique Factorization Domain (UFD) and irreducible
rubrics_metrics.description: In an integral domain R, a nonzero non-unit is irreducible if it cannot be written as the product of two non-units. R is a UFD if every nonzero non-unit can be written as a product of irreducibles, and this factorization is unique up to multiplication by units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Z is a UFD; Q[x], Z[x], Z[i] are UFDs; Z[√-5] is a classic non-example (6 admits two distinct irreducible factorizations). Theorem: Every PID is a UFD. Exercises: verify Z is a UFD, and reason about uniqueness up to units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean domain (definition via Euclidean norm)
rubrics_metrics.description: An integral domain R is a Euclidean domain if there exists a function N: R → Z_{≥0} (Euclidean norm) such that (i) N outputs nonnegative integer values (so algorithm terminates) and (ii) for any a,b ∈ R with b ≠ 0, there exists q ∈ R with remainder r = a − qb satisfying N(r) < N(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This norm allows a division-with-remainder algorithm (Euclidean algorithm) to compute gcds. Examples: Z with absolute value, Z[i] with norm a^2+b^2, Z[ω] with norm a^2+ab+b^2, Q[x] with degree as norm. Consequence: every Euclidean domain is a PID (hence a UFD). Remarks and exercises: construct q by nearest lattice point argument in Z[i]; counterexamples where no Euclidean norm exists (e.g. certain rings) are discussed via 'universal side divisor' arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal side divisor / side divisor (auxiliary concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: A side divisor of a is an element b such that there exists q with a − bq equal to 0 or a unit. A universal side divisor is a b that is a side divisor of every element a ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma: in a Euclidean domain, the smallest-norm nonzero non-unit is a universal side divisor (run the Euclidean algorithm one step). This notion is used to show certain rings (e.g. Z[(1+√-19)/2]) cannot be Euclidean by proving they have no universal side divisor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noetherian vs Artinian remarks & problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Artinian rings satisfy the descending chain condition (no infinite descending chains of ideals). It is stated that if a ring is Artinian then it is Noetherian (Akizuki's theorem mentioned as a problem), and that prime ideals in Artinian rings are maximal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problems and pointers: show implications in special cases (e.g. finite integral domains are fields), use Zorn's lemma or Noetherian property to find maximal ideals, and explore Spec of polynomial rings. These are presented as harder problems for further study.
